messages.author: 78954c94ee92247d
messages.subject: summary.scanone() chromosome specificity
parts:
Currently the summary function of a scanone object reports only the QTL with the highest LOD on each chromosome. Is there a way generate the same output but containing all the QTL in the genome that pass a certain threshold regardless of linkage?

Thanks
JC

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] summary.scanone() chromosome specificity
parts:
The difficulty is in defining peaks. When you say, "containing all the QTL in the genome that pass…", what do you mean by "QTL"?

If you want all positions with LOD above 3.5,

output[output[,3] > 3.5,]

but that could be a very long listing.

Most importantly, though, I think that proper investigation of multiple linked QTL requires the consideration of multiple-QTL models.

karl

messages.author: 78954c94ee92247d
messages.subject: Re: summary.scanone() chromosome specificity
parts:
Well, I guess as it is, the summary.scanone() function outputs the marker with the highest LOD in the linkage group, but what I was wondering is if there is a way to define (and output as in summary.scanone) a QTL as: in any linkage group a QTL is defined by the marker with the highest LOD between the closest two flanking markers that do not cross the threshold. 

I am using addqtl() and stepwiseqtl() as well as scanone() to consider a multiple QTL model, but I want to be able to put in the most information I can into the models those functions start out with. If there is evidence for a second QTL on a chromosome (from scanone() ) are you saying these other functions will identify it even if I don't include it in the qtl object populated by summary.scanone()?

Thanks.
JC

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] summary.scanone() chromosome specificity
parts:
Say you see two peaks in the scanone result and you pick off the biggest one as a QTL and then run addqtl on that chromosome. If the second peak goes away after conditioning on the first peak, what would you say? I'd probably be satisfied with the one QTL.

Consider also item 21 in the FAQ (http://www.rqtl.org/faq):

Q: How can I pick out multiple peaks on a chromosome from the output of scanone?

A: It is best not to rely on the results of scanone to infer the presence of multiple linked QTL. Instead, one should consider the results of a two-dimensional, two-QTL scan (with scantwo) or multiple QTL analysis (with fitqtl and/or scanqtl).

Nevertheless, if there are a couple of peaks on a chromosome, and one wishes to identify the location of the second peak, one can subset the results fromscanone to find the location of the second peak. For example, if out contains the output from scanone, and one wishes to find the location for the peak on chromosome 1 that is distal to 50 cM on the genetic map, one may use code like the following.

> max(out[out$chr==1 & out$pos > 50,])

karl
